analysis.title: US Economics Analyst: October FOMC Preview: Hiking at a Slower Pace
key_insights: GS expects the FOMC to skip a hike at its October meeting and deliver a second and final hike in December. Participant comments since September point to a compromise of raising the funds rate every other meeting.

Governor Waller said hikes 'do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time.' Participants have said they do not see 'urgency' for additional hikes.

GS's Financial Conditions Index has tightened by 30bp since September. That is only a bit more than is usually associated with one 25bp hike and much less than the four hikes the market has priced, so the FOMC is unlikely to see it as excessive or as a replacement for hikes.
Before September the FCI was little changed in 2026 because higher rates were offset by higher stock prices and narrower credit spreads.

A key October question is how the statement modifies the sentence on the September hike. GS thinks the Committee might adapt Vice Chair Jefferson's language: 'Any further adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate to support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal will depend on trends in the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.'
If Chairman Warsh views the Jefferson-style language as too close to past forward guidance, an alternative is to say nothing about the policy outlook in the statement.

GS does not expect significant new information from the press conference. Strong support for hiking every other meeting implies a high bar to deviate through year-end. Warsh did not hint at the slower pace at his September press conference and may again leave that to others.
Warsh could give an initial update on his task forces' work, but GS thinks it is too early for final conclusions.

On an every-other-meeting pace the next hike after December would come in March 2027, with five more months of inflation data. GS does not expect a March hike because it expects inflation to improve as tariff, energy shock and AI price effects fade.
GS estimates tariffs, the Iran energy shock and the mismeasured part of AI price pressures account for all of core PCE inflation's current 1.1pp overshoot of the 2% target.

Tariffs: incremental passthrough to consumer prices from earlier tariff rounds is essentially over, so year-on-year inflation should keep falling on base effects. Replacement of tariffs overturned by the courts should have only a modest impact.

Energy: higher oil prices and refined product spreads have lifted core PCE inflation by 0.3pp so far and would add 0.1-0.15pp under the GS baseline. Oil futures are above GS forecasts on concern about further Middle East conflict, which is the clearest upside risk to the inflation forecast.
If oil follows the futures curve, GS would add another 0.1pp to its core PCE forecast by March and about 0.4pp to its headline forecast.

AI price pressures: the impact on year-over-year core PCE is likely to peak over the next few months and fall meaningfully in 2027 as memory and computer price growth slows. Monthly memory price effects have been erratic, so near-term uncertainty remains.

A longer or more extreme energy shock raises the risk of a larger 'January effect' as firms pass on higher costs with start-of-year price increases, hitting the second-to-last inflation print before the March meeting.
Prices-received components of business surveys have risen substantially in manufacturing but remain at more normal levels in services.

Some participants may share GS's view that the economy is not overheated and the overshoot from past supply shocks must largely be waited out, and may prefer to limit the total size of the hiking cycle. Concerns about growth or employment would likely end hikes.

Market pricing has removed one hike since end-September. It peaks at about 4.55% in fall 2027, implying just under three more hikes for a total of four. GS's baseline and probability-weighted paths are considerably less hawkish.

risk_factors: Oil futures above GS forecasts on Middle East conflict risk, the clearest upside risk to the inflation forecast.
A larger January effect from start-of-year price increases if the energy shock lasts.
Inflation broadening beyond manufacturing into services price surveys.
Month-to-month erratic AI-driven memory price effects on consumer prices.
Growth or employment weakness, for example from higher energy prices eroding real income or a larger tightening in financial conditions, would likely end hikes.
charts_described: Exhibit 1 plots changes in the GS US FCI since January 1, 2026 with contributions from the 10-year Treasury, fed funds, BBB credit spread, S&P 500 and dollar TWI, alongside the peak fed funds rate priced for 2027.
Exhibit 3 shows tariff, energy/Iran and software and accessories effects on year-over-year core PCE, which GS says account for the current 1.1pp overshoot of the 2% target.

Exhibit 4 shows the estimated impact of commodity prices on year-over-year core PCE: a 0.3pp boost so far and another 0.1-0.15pp under the GS oil forecast, or 0.25pp if oil follows the higher futures curve.
Exhibit 7 shows GS fed funds scenarios: three hikes with a higher terminal rate (35%), two hikes then cuts to 3.25-3.5% (GS baseline, 50%), and recession (15%).
geopolitical: Concern about potential further conflict with Iran is pushing oil futures above GS forecasts and is the main upside risk to the inflation outlook.
An Iran-related energy shock is cited as one of three drivers of the core PCE overshoot.
The White House is replacing earlier tariffs that were overturned by the courts, which should lift the effective tariff rate slightly.

tension_points.bull_case: Hawkish case: market prices four hikes, and a March 2027 hike is possible if inflation runs worse than GS expects, with oil futures above GS forecasts and a possible January effect.
tension_points.bear_case: GS expects the hiking cycle to end in December. Tariff, energy and AI price effects should fade, the economy is not overheated, and growth or employment concerns would likely end hikes.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Oil prices following the futures curve above GS forecasts, or worse inflation prints through the March meeting, would make a March hike possible.
